title: IELTS Academic Writing — Practice Test 26
topics: The commercial production of olive oil, from harvest to bottling
A four-day working week for all employees

task1.prompt:
The diagram below shows the stages involved in producing olive oil commercially, from harvesting the olives to bottling the finished oil.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

stages.name: Harvesting
stages.description: Ripe olives are shaken or raked from the trees between October and December and collected in nets or crates. They are delivered to the mill within 24 hours to prevent fermentation.

stages.name: Leaf removal and washing
stages.description: A blower strips away leaves and twigs, and the olives pass through a cold-water wash that removes soil, dust and any chemical residue.

stages.name: Crushing
stages.description: Whole olives, including stones, are ground into a thick paste by a hammer mill or traditional stone wheels.

stages.name: Malaxation
stages.description: The paste is slowly stirred for 30 to 45 minutes at no more than 27°C so that tiny oil droplets merge into larger ones.

stages.name: Centrifugal separation
stages.description: A horizontal centrifuge (decanter) spins the paste at high speed, separating the oil from the water and the solid pomace. The pomace is removed as a by-product.

stages.name: Filtration
stages.description: The cloudy oil passes through cellulose or cotton filters to remove remaining water and fruit particles, giving a clear, stable product.

stages.name: Storage
stages.description: The filtered oil rests in sealed stainless-steel tanks under nitrogen, at 15–18°C and away from light, for up to several months.

stages.name: Bottling
stages.description: Oil is drawn from the tanks and bottled in dark glass or tins, labelled with the harvest date, and packed for distribution to retailers.

task2.prompt:
Some governments are considering introducing a four-day working week for all employees, with no reduction in pay.

Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?

ta: Gives a clear overview that states the number of stages (eight), the start and end points (harvested fruit to labelled bottles) and the broad shape of the process: preparation, extraction, then refining and storage.
Reports all the stages in sequence without omitting the less obvious ones such as leaf removal or malaxation; a Band 8+ answer also notes the by-product (pomace) separated at stage 5.

Includes the specific details that the diagram offers — the 24-hour delivery window, the 27°C limit, the 30–45 minute stirring, the 15–18°C storage — and uses them to show how strictly the process is controlled.
Stays descriptive: no explanation of why cold pressing improves flavour, and no personal opinion about olive oil quality.
cc: Organises the stages into two or three logical body paragraphs (e.g. stages 1–3 preparation and crushing; 4–5 extraction; 6–8 finishing) instead of one sentence per stage in a single block.
Uses sequencing language that varies and does work — "once", "after which", "at this point", "the final stage" — rather than "then… then… then".
Refers back to the product as it changes state (olives → paste → cloudy oil → clear oil) so that the reader can follow what is being handled at each step.
lr: Uses precise process vocabulary: harvested, stripped, ground into a paste, stirred, separated by centrifugal force, filtered, stored under nitrogen, bottled and labelled.
Paraphrases the diagram labels where natural ("leaf removal" → "leaves and twigs are blown away") rather than copying every label verbatim.
Distinguishes between by-products and the main product (pomace, water versus oil) with accurate collocations such as "removed as waste" and "drawn off".
gra: Uses the present simple passive consistently and accurately ("the olives are washed", "the paste is stirred"), switching to active only where the agent matters ("a centrifuge separates…").
Controls complex sentences with time clauses and participles ("Having been crushed, the paste is…"; "before the oil is filtered, it…").
Punctuates figures and units correctly (27°C, 30–45 minutes, 15–18°C) and keeps the majority of sentences error-free.

ta: Answers the actual question — whether the advantages outweigh the disadvantages — with a clear judgement stated in the introduction and sustained, not merely a list of pros and cons.
Engages with the specific proposal: a universal four-day week with no pay cut. A strong essay considers who this suits (office work) and who it does not (hospitals, transport, small retailers).
Develops each side with concrete reasoning, e.g. the evidence on productivity and staff retention versus the cost to employers and the risk of compressed ten-hour days.
Weighs the two sides explicitly in the conclusion rather than ending with "there are both advantages and disadvantages".
cc: A clear structure: introduction with position, one paragraph on benefits, one on drawbacks, and a conclusion that returns to the weighing — or a position-first structure that deals with drawbacks before the stronger benefits.
Each body paragraph has a single controlling idea and a topic sentence; supporting sentences extend it rather than introducing unrelated points.
Cohesion comes from logical sequencing and referencing ("this shift", "such a policy", "these sectors") rather than a mechanical linker opening every sentence.
lr: Uses precise work-related vocabulary: productivity, burnout, staff retention, compressed hours, operating costs, service sectors, work-life balance, legislation versus voluntary adoption.
Paraphrases the prompt naturally ("four-day working week" → "a shorter working week", "a reduction in working days") without distorting its meaning.
Less common collocations used accurately ("a blanket policy", "round-the-clock services", "absorb the cost", "take-up") and a consistently formal register.
gra: Handles conditionals and hypothetical language the topic demands ("If such a policy were imposed on hospitals…", "employers would have to…") accurately.
Uses concession structures to weigh points ("Although the productivity gains are real, …", "While this is true of office work, …").
Varies sentence length and type; comma use around subordinate clauses is correct and errors are rare and do not impede meaning.

traps.title: Skipping malaxation
traps.detail: Candidates often jump from crushing straight to separation because the stirring stage looks minor. It is a distinct step with its own figures (30–45 minutes, under 27°C) and omitting it means the process is reported incompletely, which limits Task Achievement.

traps.title: Forgetting the by-product
traps.detail: Stage 5 produces two outputs: the oil that continues, and the pomace that leaves the process. A Band 7+ answer mentions what is removed, not only what goes forward.

traps.title: Writing in the past or the active voice throughout
traps.detail: A process diagram describes what routinely happens, so the present simple passive is the natural choice. "Farmers harvested the olives and then they crushed them" reads as a narrative, not a process description.

traps.title: Overview that is only a count
traps.detail: "There are eight stages" is not an overview on its own. Add the start and end products and the overall shape of the process (preparation → extraction → refining and storage).

traps.title: Explaining the chemistry
traps.detail: Describing why low temperatures preserve flavour or what polyphenols are is irrelevant to Task 1 and spends words that should go on the diagram's information.

traps.title: Answering a different question
traps.detail: The prompt asks whether advantages outweigh disadvantages. Essays that simply list both sides, or that argue only about whether the policy is a good idea, do not answer the weighing question and are capped on Task Response.

traps.title: Ignoring 'all employees' and 'no reduction in pay'
traps.detail: These two details are what make the question hard. An essay about flexible working in offices misses the point; the strongest answers ask what happens to nurses, bus drivers and shop staff, and who pays for the fifth day.

traps.title: Sitting on the fence
traps.detail: "It depends on the company" is a reasonable observation but not a position. State clearly whether, on balance, the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, and defend that view.
